new_statements.quote: The phoneme inventory of Bit is introduced in Table 1 below (Badenoch 2015). Bit has 10 simple vowels, all contrasting for length, and four diphthongs. [...] Bit is a disyllabic, iambic language, with many onset clusters and a rich system of morphology.
new_statements.citation: Badenoch, Nathan. 2016. Bit Personal Pronouns in a Northern Mon-Khmer Context. Annals of Foreign Studies (神戸市外国語大学外国学研究) 92: 5-23. Kobe City University of Foreign Studies.
new_statements.locator: Sec. 0 Introduction, p. 6 (PDF page 2), immediately after Table 2 'Bit consonants'
new_statements.rule_in_words: Bit words are mono- or sesquisyllabic ('disyllabic' in Badenoch's usage: a minor syllable plus a major syllable) and iambic, i.e. prominence falls on the final (major) syllable; the language is atonal. This matches the second-hand summary in Sidwell 2015: 55 (via Wikipedia): 'Stress falls on the final syllable', template (C1(ə(C2))).ˈCi(Cm)V(ː)(Cf).
new_statements.exceptions: None mentioned; compounding and expressive formations can yield true disyllables (per Sidwell 2015 summary), with no statement on their stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word (lexical items in citation form and text data from Ban Bompiang, Luang Namtha, Laos, 2011-2015). The statement is a one-line typological characterisation ('iambic'), not an explicit stress rule; the fuller sketch is the unpublished Badenoch 2015 SEALS 25 paper as summarised in Sidwell 2015: 55-57.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement describes Bit of Ban Bompiang, Luang Namtha, Laos (Badenoch's fieldwork 2011-2015); Badenoch treats Chinese Buxing (Gao 2004; Mengla, Yunnan) as a closely related dialect of the same language, so it applies to bitt1240 as a whole. Two of the four Glottolog 5.1 references for bitt1240 (Tạ 2021, Tạ 2023) actually describe Kháng of Vietnam (ISO kjm, Glottolog khan1274), a tonal sister language in the same Khao subgroup — not Bit; the earlier world scan's note '(= Bit [bgk] variety)' is wrong on that point.

sources.locator: Sec. 0 Introduction, p. 6 (PDF page 2), immediately after Table 2 'Bit consonants'
sources.note: Sec. 0 Introduction, p. 6: phoneme inventory (Tables 1-2, citing Badenoch 2015) then 'Bit is a disyllabic, iambic language, with many onset clusters and a rich system of morphology.' No separate stress rule; data = Ban Bompiang, Luang Namtha, Laos, 2011-2015; also notes minor syllables (/CrC/) and that Bit is atonal while related Bumang developed tones.

sources.citation: Wikipedia, 'Bit language' (wikitext retrieved 2026-09-17), phonology section citing Sidwell 2015: 55-57 and Badenoch 2015/2016.
sources.note: Second-hand: 'Bit/Buxing phonological word can be mono- or sesquisyllabic... Stress falls on the final syllable. No tones or registers were reported. The phonological template is (C1(ə(C2))).ˈCi(Cm)V(ː)(Cf).' attributed to Sidwell 2015 p. 55 (Laotian Bit data from Badenoch).

sources.citation: Glottolog 5.1 languoid page bitt1240 (Bit) and languoid page for ISO kjm (Kháng, khan1274).
sources.note: Classification Austroasiatic > Palaungic > East Palaungic > Khao > Bit; Kháng is a separate languoid (khan1274, kjm). Glottolog nonetheless files Ta 2021/2023 (Kháng) under bitt1240's references.
